issues.legal_issue: A review of a High Court decision made in original writ jurisdiction retains the character of that jurisdiction.
material_facts: The decision sought to be reviewed was made by a High Court Division Bench in a public interest writ petition under Article 226.
A party applied to the same High Court for review of that decision.
issues.conclusion: The review proceedings partook of the original jurisdiction exercised when the underlying writ decision was made; review was not an independent jurisdiction distinct from that original jurisdiction.
issues.legal_principle: Review is a request to the same court to reconsider its decision within the limits of review jurisdiction, not an appeal to a superior court. The jurisdiction exercised on review takes its character from the jurisdiction exercised in the decision under review. The Court relied on Order XLVII Rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC), and Clause 36 of the Letters Patent.

predicates.review_of_original_writ_decision: A party seeks review in the same High Court of a decision that the High Court made in an original writ proceeding.

issues.definition: When a party seeks review in the same High Court of its decision in an original writ proceeding, the review retains the character of the original jurisdiction.

issues.legal_issue: When two judges disagree in review proceedings arising from an original writ decision, the differing points must be referred to another judge under the applicable High Court charter rather than the review petition being dismissed for lack of a majority.
material_facts: A two-judge High Court bench heard a review petition arising from a decision in an Article 226 writ proceeding.
The judges disagreed on the review petition, including on whether the applicant was covered by the directions in the original decision.
The High Court dismissed the review petition under Order XLVII Rule 6 of the CPC instead of referring the points of disagreement to another judge.
issues.conclusion: The dismissal could not stand. The review petition was restored, and the points on which the judges differed or did not concur, whether questions of fact or law, were to be referred to a third judge under Clause 36 of the Letters Patent.
issues.legal_principle: Clause 36 of the Letters Patent governs disagreement in a Division Bench reviewing a decision made in original jurisdiction and requires the unresolved points to be heard by another judge, with the outcome determined according to the majority opinion. The Court held that Section 98(2) of the CPC, which concerns confirmation of a lower court's decree, does not apply to review proceedings arising from an original writ decision; Section 98(3) preserves the Letters Patent procedure. Rule 186 of the Gujarat High Court Rules refers to the procedure in Section 98 but does not displace Clause 36. Sections 4(1) and 129 of the CPC also support the application of the charter procedure, which cannot be cut down by inconsistent CPC provisions. Order XLVII Rule 6 therefore did not justify dismissal. The Court relied on Bhaidas Shivdas v. Bai Gulba, AIR 1921 Privy Council 6, concerning the precedence of the Letters Patent procedure over a conflicting CPC procedure.

predicates.review_of_original_writ_decision: A party seeks review in the same High Court of a decision that the High Court made in an original writ proceeding.
predicates.two_judge_review_bench_disagrees: Two judges hearing the review do not agree on one or more points requiring decision.
predicates.high_court_charter_provides_split_bench_: The High Court is governed by a charter that provides for referral when judges on a bench disagree.

issues.definition: If a two-judge bench disagrees while reviewing the High Court's original writ decision and the High Court's governing charter provides for referral, the unresolved points must be referred to another judge.
